hero.name: Vivek
hero.who: a 24-year-old in Bhopal who has switched paths three times and feels behind

story.h: What are you doing these days?
story.b: Vivek is twenty-four and has already switched paths three times. One year of hotel management. A course in mobile repair. Eight months selling insurance door to door. Now he helps at his father's small printing press in old Bhopal, printing wedding cards and shop bills. At every family function, an aunty asks what he is doing these days, and he mumbles something. His cousin chose biology at fifteen and is now a doctor. Vivek feels he has wasted years while everyone else ran in a straight line. He thinks about cramming for a government exam he has no interest in, just to stop the questions. Quietly, he wonders if it is too late for anything.

ask.q: Vivek feels his years of switching were a waste. Which view would help him most?
o: His years of trying things are useful experience, not wasted time
He should lock into any one path now and never switch again
He has fallen behind for good, so he should lower his hopes
ask.why: Comparing his path with a cousin who chose early makes his detours look like failure. Locking into anything just to stop switching risks a poor fit, and lowering his hopes ignores what he has learned. His sampling has already shown him what suits him and what does not.

chapters.take: A winding path is not a wasted one.

story.b: At the press, Vivek's father teaches him to align the printing plates. It is a clear task. Get it wrong and the ink smudges at once, so practice quickly makes him better. Within a month his cards come out sharp. But the other side of the business is murkier. Which card designs will sell this wedding season? How much should they charge a new hotel client? Feedback there takes months, and the rules keep changing. Vivek notices that his drilled skills do not help with this. What helps is everything else. The hotel course taught him how guests think, and insurance taught him how to read a hesitant customer. Those messy years suddenly feel useful.

ask.q: Vivek wants to get better at guessing which designs customers will want next season. What will help most?
o: Repeat last season's best design until it is absolutely perfect
Copy exactly what the biggest press in town is doing
Talk to many different customers and test a range of ideas
ask.why: Aligning plates is a clear task where repetition and quick feedback build skill. Guessing future demand is messy, with slow feedback and shifting rules, so polishing one design or copying another shop gives false confidence. Wide exposure and flexible testing work better there.

chapters.take: Drills win where rules are clear. Breadth wins where they keep changing.

story.b: Vivek's uncle tells him to sit the government exam and settle down. Vivek is tempted, because settled sounds peaceful. Instead he gives himself three months of small, cheap experiments. He takes a short evening course in graphic design. On weekends he helps a friend who decorates wedding venues. He designs a menu card for free for a dhaba near the bus stand, just to see how it feels. The design course surprises him. He forgets to check the time. The decoration work is fun but exhausting. The dhaba owner loves his menu and sends two more shops his way. By the end of the three months, Vivek knows much better what fits him.

ask.q: Vivek's uncle says he should take the government exam and stop wasting time. What should Vivek do?
o: Take the exam route anyway, because a settled job ends the questions
Try a few short, low-cost projects first to see what truly fits
Ignore everyone and switch to something new whenever he feels bored
ask.why: A path chosen just to stop questions may be a poor fit for years. Switching whenever he is bored is not real sampling, because he learns little from each. Short, deliberate trials let him test what suits him before he commits.

chapters.take: Try a few things on purpose before you settle on one.

story.b: In the design course, Vivek watches each tutorial video two or three times. By the end he feels he knows the software well. Then a customer asks for a wedding card with a new layout, and Vivek freezes in front of the screen. He cannot remember which tool does what. So he changes how he practises. Before watching a lesson, he tries the task from memory and gets stuck. He mixes his practice, a logo on Monday, a poster on Tuesday, a card on Wednesday. He comes back to each tool after a few days, when it has half faded. It is slower and more frustrating. But the next real customer job goes smoothly.

ask.q: A friend learning design with Vivek says rewatching tutorials feels faster. What should Vivek tell him?
o: Rewatch until every step feels familiar, then start real work
Stick to one type of design until it feels smooth
Try tasks from memory first and mix different kinds of work
ask.why: Rewatching feels productive, but familiar is not the same as able. Practising only one kind of design feels smooth yet does not carry over to new jobs. Struggling to recall and mixing tasks feels slower, but it builds skill that holds up with real customers.

chapters.take: Learning that feels slow and mixed often lasts the longest.

story.h: A kitchen rail at the press
story.b: Wedding season hits the press like a storm. Customers crowd the counter, orders get mixed up, and one family receives cards with another family's names. Vivek's father says every press has this mess. Vivek thinks of something else. During his hotel management year, he saw a busy restaurant kitchen handle hundreds of orders a night with order slips clipped to a steel rail, read from left to right. He buys a cheap rail and some clips. Every order gets a slip, coloured by delivery date, and moves along the rail as it is printed. From his insurance days he adds a follow-up call the day before pickup. The counter calms down within a week.

ask.q: The press keeps losing track of orders in wedding season. Where should Vivek look for a fix?
o: At how a completely different business, like a restaurant kitchen, handles orders
Only at what other printing presses in Bhopal already do
Nowhere, since every printing press just has a messy season
ask.why: Other presses likely share the same blind spots, and accepting the mess solves nothing. A distant field, like a kitchen that handles hundreds of orders every night, can offer a ready pattern. Breadth gives him more ideas to borrow.

chapters.take: The best fix for your problem may live in a completely different field.

story.b: Vivek's friend Ritu calls one night. She is twenty-eight, works as an accountant, and dreams of running a plant nursery, but feels it is far too late. Vivek understands, because he felt the same at twenty-four. Before answering, he shows her a list he made last month. Skills from his detours. Hotel management taught him service and order systems. Mobile repair taught him patience with tiny details. Insurance taught him to talk to strangers and follow up. Every one of them makes him a better designer for real customers. He asks Ritu to make her own list. She writes costing, records and handling suppliers, and suddenly the nursery feels a little closer.

ask.q: Ritu, twenty-eight, wants to leave accounting for a plant nursery but feels too late. What should Vivek tell her?
o: Stay put, since switching now would waste her accounting degree
Her accounting skills can help a nursery, and late starts are normal
Quit tomorrow and forget about money, since dreams matter most
ask.why: Many people find their real work after a few turns, and her accounting years bring skills like costing and records that a nursery needs. Staying put out of fear ignores a poor fit, while quitting with no plan is reckless. A thoughtful switch that uses her past works best.

chapters.take: Your detours are not lost years. They are the skills you bring.

story.h: The design desk by the window
story.b: By the next wedding season, the press has a new corner. Vivek's design desk sits by the window, with a laptop, sample cards and the steel order rail behind it. His father now lets him price new jobs. Vivek still learns each new tool by trying it before watching the video. The dhaba owner's friends keep sending work. At his cousin's engagement, an aunty asks the old question, what is he doing these days. Vivek answers easily. He designs, runs the front of the press, and might try more later. His doctor cousin overhears and asks him to design the board for her new clinic. Vivek takes out his phone and fixes a time.

chapters.take: Explore widely, learn deeply, and let every detour feed the next step.
